question:
Use the Weave documentation at https://docs.wandb.ai/weave to answer this question:

How do tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together?
answer:
In Weave, tracing records what your agent or app does. Evaluations test it against fixed test cases before you ship changes. Signals score the agent conversations you trace in production. Weave describes itself as an observability and evaluation platform that helps you see what your AI app is doing, measure how well it works and improve it over time [S3].

- **Tracing (seeing what happens):** Weave shows you agent sessions and multi-turn conversations, or the individual function calls in your code [S6]. There are two ways to trace. *Agent tracing* is for agents, and those traces appear on the **Agents** page. *Application instrumentation* is for code built around separate calls, such as a RAG pipeline (an app that looks up documents before answering). These `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page. You can use both in one project, but they create separate traces [S4].
- **Evaluations (testing before you ship):** An `Evaluation` object combines a dataset of test examples with one or more scoring functions. You run it against a model or function, and each `.evaluate()` call creates an evaluation run [S2]. Use this to measure performance on repeatable test cases, compare changes over time and catch regressions (results that get worse after a change) [S2]. It also tracks which model and prompt versions produced which results [S8].
- **Signals (monitoring in production):** Signals score agent turns. In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals can automatically score answer quality, notice when a user is frustrated or flag NSFW content. They point you to the traces that need attention [S1]. A *turn* is one exchange between the user and the agent. A *rating* is a score from 0.0 to 1.0, and a *tag* is a label such as "user-frustration". Both ratings and tags are assigned to matching spans, which are parts of a trace [S5]. To view them, select your project in Forge, then **Agents**, then the **Signals** tab [S7].

**How they connect (my inference):** You need agent tracing first, because Signals score the conversations shown in the Agents view. Signals then help you find problem conversations in live traffic. Evaluations check, in a controlled way, whether a fix actually helps, since they rerun the same test cases each time. Together this matches Weave's goals of visibility, systematic evaluation and production monitoring [S6].

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

# What is Weave?

> Learn about W&B Weave and how it helps you build, evaluate, and improve LLM applications

W\&B Weave is an observability and evaluation platform for building reliable agents and LLM applications. Weave helps you understand what your AI application is doing, measure how well it performs, and systematically improve it over time.

Building LLM applications is fundamentally different from traditional software development. LLM outputs are non-deterministic, making debugging harder. Quality is subjective and context-dependent. Small prompt changes can cause unexpected behavior changes. Traditional testing approaches fall short.

sources.text:
### When to use agent tracing and when to use application instrumentation

Choose which workflow to use based on what you want to observe:

* **Use agent tracing if you're building or running an agent.** This is the right fit if you use a supported agent harness or agent SDK, or if you've built a custom agent that you can instrument yourself.

* **Use application instrumentation if you're tracing application code.** This is the right fit for applications structured around discrete calls rather than conversations, such as a RAG pipeline, a summarization endpoint, or custom business logic.

Each approach records traces in its own part of the UI: agent traces appear on the **Agents** page, and `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page. You can use both approaches in the same Weave project, but they produce separate traces.

If you're not sure where to start and your system involves an agent, start with agent tracing using the [agent integration quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/agent-integration-quickstart.md). Otherwise, start with the [Op tracing quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/quickstart.md).

sources.text:
## Core capabilities

Weave provides the following core functionality:

* **Visibility** into agent sessions and multi-turn conversations, or into individual function calls and outputs in application code.
* **Systematic evaluation** to measure performance against curated test cases.
* **Version tracking** for prompts, models, and data so you can understand what changed.
* **Experimentation** with different prompt and model comparisons.
* **Feedback collection** to capture human judgments and annotations.
* **Monitoring** in production using guardrails and scorers for LLM safety and quality.

all_read_evidence.text:
### When to use agent tracing and when to use application instrumentation

Choose which workflow to use based on what you want to observe:

* **Use agent tracing if you're building or running an agent.** This is the right fit if you use a supported agent harness or agent SDK, or if you've built a custom agent that you can instrument yourself.

* **Use application instrumentation if you're tracing application code.** This is the right fit for applications structured around discrete calls rather than conversations, such as a RAG pipeline, a summarization endpoint, or custom business logic.

Each approach records traces in its own part of the UI: agent traces appear on the **Agents** page, and `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page. You can use both approaches in the same Weave project, but they produce separate traces.

If you're not sure where to start and your system involves an agent, start with agent tracing using the [agent integration quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/agent-integration-quickstart.md). Otherwise, start with the [Op tracing quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/quickstart.md).

## Core capabilities

Weave provides the following core functionality:

* **Visibility** into agent sessions and multi-turn conversations, or into individual function calls and outputs in application code.
* **Systematic evaluation** to measure performance against curated test cases.
* **Version tracking** for prompts, models, and data so you can understand what changed.
* **Experimentation** with different prompt and model comparisons.
* **Feedback collection** to capture human judgments and annotations.
* **Monitoring** in production using guardrails and scorers for LLM safety and quality.

In Weave, tracing records what your agent or app does. Evaluations test it against fixed test cases before you ship changes. Signals score the agent conversations you trace in production. Weave describes itself as an observability and evaluation platform that helps you see what your AI app is doing, measure how well it works and improve it over time [S3].

- **Tracing (seeing what happens):** Weave shows you agent sessions and multi-turn conversations, or the individual function calls in your code [S6]. There are two ways to trace. *Agent tracing* is for agents, and those traces appear on the **Agents** page. *Application instrumentation* is for code built around separate calls, such as a RAG pipeline (an app that looks up documents before answering). These `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page. You can use both in one project, but they create separate traces [S4].
- **Evaluations (testing before you ship):** An `Evaluation` object combines a dataset of test examples with one or more scoring functions. You run it against a model or function, and each `.evaluate()` call creates an evaluation run [S2]. Use this to measure performance on repeatable test cases, compare changes over time and catch regressions (results that get worse after a change) [S2]. It also tracks which model and prompt versions produced which results [S8].
- **Signals (monitoring in production):** In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals can automatically score answer quality, notice when a user is frustrated or flag NSFW content. They point you to the traces that need attention [S1]. Evaluations check, in a controlled way, whether a fix actually helps, since they rerun the same test cases each time. results.title: Monitor using built-in signals
results.heading: Available signals
results.snippet:
## Available signals

Weave offers monitors with built-in signals: preset scorers that evaluate production traces for common quality issues and errors by default, with no custom setup. Each built-in signal uses a benchmarked LLM prompt to classify traces and saves the results as comma-delimited tags representing the detected issues.

Signals use a [Serverless Inference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/inference/serverless.md) model to score traces, so you don't need external API keys.

Weave provides 13 preset signals organized into two groups.

Use [signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/monitors.md), preset automated scorers for production traces, to get started with production monitoring quickly, then add custom monitors for evaluation criteria specific to your application.

> Evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics with Weave Scorers

In Weave, Scorers evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics. They take the AI's output, analyze it, and return a dictionary of results. Scorers can use your input data as reference if needed and can also output extra information, such as explanations or reasoning from the evaluation.

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

After you run an agent with the exporter enabled, Koog forwards traces to your Weave project. Koog's Weave exporter captures the same spans as Koog's general OTEL integration, including:

In Weave, tracing records what your agent or app does. Evaluations test it against fixed test cases before you ship changes. Signals score the agent conversations you trace in production. Weave describes itself as an observability and evaluation platform that helps you see what your AI app is doing, measure how well it works and improve it over time [S3].

- **Tracing (seeing what happens):** Weave shows you agent sessions and multi-turn conversations, or the individual function calls in your code [S6]. There are two ways to trace. *Agent tracing* is for agents, and those traces appear on the **Agents** page. *Application instrumentation* is for code built around separate calls, such as a RAG pipeline (an app that looks up documents before answering). These `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page. You can use both in one project, but they create separate traces [S4].
- **Evaluations (testing before you ship):** An `Evaluation` object combines a dataset of test examples with one or more scoring functions. You run it against a model or function, and each `.evaluate()` call creates an evaluation run [S2]. Use this to measure performance on repeatable test cases, compare changes over time and catch regressions (results that get worse after a change) [S2]. It also tracks which model and prompt versions produced which results [S8].
- **Signals (monitoring in production):** In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals can automatically score answer quality, notice when a user is frustrated or flag NSFW content. They point you to the traces that need attention [S1]. A *rating* is a score from 0.0 to 1.0, and a *tag* is a label such as "user-frustration". Both are applied per *turn*, meaning one exchange between the user and the agent [S5]. To view them, select your project in Forge, then **Agents**, then the **Signals** tab [S7].

**How they connect (my inference):** You need agent tracing first, because Signals score the conversations shown in the Agents view. Signals then help you find problem conversations in live traffic. Evaluations check, in a controlled way, whether a fix actually helps, since they rerun the same test cases each time. Together this matches Weave's goals of visibility, systematic evaluation and production monitoring [S6].
